slides.title: Texture Mapping as Lookup
slides.notes: Open the lecture by separating the informal phrase put the image on the object from the computation that actually happens. The renderer starts at a visible surface point, evaluates a texture coordinate function, filters the texture signal, and only then uses that value in shading or geometry.

slides.title: The Two Fundamental Problems
slides.notes: Frame the whole chapter as a compact decision tree. First ask how a point on the surface gets coordinates in the texture domain. Then ask what part of the texture a pixel covers and how the renderer should average it. Later applications reuse exactly these answers.

slides.title: Lookup Direction
slides.notes: Emphasize the direction of dependency in a shader. The visible point is already known from ray tracing or rasterization, so texture mapping asks the surface where to sample. This mental model helps students debug wrong wrap modes, wrong transforms, and inverted coordinate conventions.

slides.title: Coordinate Functions
slides.notes: Use this slide to connect texture mapping to cartography. The renderer needs a practical coordinate function, but the map is never free: injectivity, area scale, local shape, and continuity compete. The examples are deliberately schematic so students focus on tradeoffs rather than on a specific asset.

slides.title: Mesh Atlases
slides.notes: Explain that mesh UVs turn a global mapping problem into many small affine maps. Each triangle can be simple, while the atlas layout decides where seams, overlaps, and density changes occur. Barycentric interpolation is familiar from rasterization, but here it interpolates coordinates used to fetch another signal.

slides.title: Seams and Wrapping
slides.notes: Walk through the seam example slowly. The two end points are close on the model but far apart in the atlas if the coordinates are interpreted literally. Duplicating vertices lets neighboring triangles choose equivalent coordinates, while wrapping modes define what texture values mean outside the unit square.

slides.title: Perspective Correct Interpolation
slides.notes: Tie this formula back to the graphics pipeline chapter. Barycentric weights are computed in screen space, but the original triangle lived in homogeneous coordinates. Interpolating u over w, v over w, and one over w is the repair that makes texture features track the projected 3D surface.

slides.title: Pixel Footprints
slides.notes: Make the key shift from point samples to areas. The local derivative of the image-to-texture mapping tells the renderer what texture region contributes to one image sample. Small footprints call for reconstruction; large footprints call for prefiltered averages; elongated footprints explain why simple mipmaps blur at grazing angles.

slides.title: Mipmaps
slides.notes: Present mipmaps as a memory-for-time tradeoff. Instead of averaging thousands of texels during a lookup, the renderer stores averages at powers of two and samples an appropriate level. The approximation is excellent for roughly square footprints and visibly over-blurry for strongly elongated ones.

slides.title: Anisotropic Filtering
slides.notes: Use the diagram to contrast what the mipmap approximation does with what the footprint actually asks for. The dashed square is easy to sample but includes too much irrelevant texture. Multiple samples along the long axis approximate the same area with better directional selectivity.

slides.title: Material Parameter Maps
slides.notes: After students understand lookup and filtering, broaden the meaning of texture. A texture may store colors, scalar coefficients, masks, or packed channels. The shader must decode the sampled values consistently, and the same filtering issues still apply because the texture is still a sampled signal.

slides.title: Normal Bump Displacement
slides.notes: Separate the three techniques by their observable consequences. Normal and bump maps alter lighting normals while the underlying surface remains smooth, so silhouettes stay unchanged. Displacement maps move geometry after tessellation, which is more expensive but changes shape, parallax, and intersections in a way shading tricks cannot.

slides.title: Shadow Maps
slides.notes: Describe the shadow map as a visibility cache from the light. The main render projects each fragment into that cache and compares depths. Bias addresses numerical disagreement between the two passes, while percentage-closer filtering averages nearby pass-fail comparisons rather than interpolating the stored depths themselves.

slides.title: Environment Maps
slides.notes: Make clear that environment maps are still texture maps, but the domain is directions. The reflected ray direction determines the lookup. Latitude-longitude storage is easy to derive and easy to visualize, while cubemaps reduce pole distortion and are common in interactive rendering systems.

slides.title: Procedural Textures
slides.notes: Use procedural textures as the endpoint of the chapter: the machinery is still about sampling a signal, but the signal need not be a stored 2D image. Solid textures are useful when the material should behave like it fills a volume, and turbulence provides multiscale irregularity without hand-painted data.

slides.title: Debugging Texture Mappings
slides.notes: Turn the notebook into a practical debugging routine. Diagnostic textures should reveal orientation, scale, and seam errors immediately. The strongest lab answers pair a visual observation with a numeric invariant, because texture bugs often look plausible until a check exposes the wrong mapping or filtering assumption.

slides.title: Texture Mapping Recap
slides.notes: Close by returning to the two foundational mechanisms from the beginning. The coordinate function decides location; the footprint and filter decide the average; the shader decides interpretation. That framing makes diffuse textures, normal maps, shadow maps, environment maps, and procedural textures feel like one coherent rendering idea.
